_comment:
The instruction a TEACHER pastes into an AI chat to build a tree. It wraps prompts/decomposition.json: this module is the context around the method -- what the teacher wants, what the site does with the file, what may be changed, how to come back and change it, and what the error messages mean -- and `leadIn` is the last section before the decomposition model itself is appended.
The point is that a teacher does exactly what a student does: paste one instruction into whichever AI chat they already use, and be taken through the work. That is why this lives here, versioned, rather than as text on one website.
title: Authoring an own skill tree

sections.role:
I am a teacher and want to build a **skill tree** for my subject: a graph of its skills and concepts, where each node says what mastering it means and which nodes must come first. My students will see the whole structure, tick off what they have mastered, and copy an AI instruction for what they want to practise next.

Take me through making one. The specification is at the end of this message; reading it is your job, not mine.
sections.oneAtATime: **Ask me one thing at a time, and wait for the answer.** No lists of questions, and no nodes before I have told you the subject. Keep any explanation to a sentence or two.
sections.whatIGetBack: At the end I need **one spreadsheet**, `tree.csv`, as the specification describes: settings at the top, one row per node below. Give me the whole file in one code block, and the whole file again after every change, never a fragment or a diff, because I save over the old one.
sections.howIUseIt: What I do with it: I drop the file into **aiskilltrees.com/make-your-own/**, which draws the tree in my own browser (nothing is uploaded), shows how it read my settings, and lists anything wrong. Then I download one HTML file holding the whole tree. It works offline with no account, and I share it with my students, who tick off nodes and copy instructions into whichever AI chat they use. The tree never talks to an AI itself.
sections.comingBack:
**I may come back later with the file**, perhaps in a new conversation, and ask for changes. Then:
- Read the file I paste before proposing anything. It, not your memory, is the truth.
- Change only what I asked for. Don't reword, reorder or "improve" anything else.
- Give me the whole file back.
- If my change breaks something (a removed node others depend on), say so and ask rather than fixing it silently.
sections.whenSomethingIsWrong:
**If the page shows errors, I will paste them to you.** They name the row and node; use them literally. The usual ones:
- *Unknown setting*: a misspelled key; the message guesses the right one.
- *A node lists a prerequisite that does not exist*: usually an id spelled differently in two rows.
- *These nodes are prerequisites for each other, in a circle*: one link has to go; tell me which you think is wrong and why.
- *The first row must name the columns*: the file was saved in the wrong format; give it again as plain CSV.
- *Unknown section in a prompt row*, or *the prompt row is aimed at something that is not an instruction*: a wrong section or instruction name (see aiskilltrees.com/prompts/). That row was not used.

One problem has no error: **a tree where almost every node has no prerequisites.** The page shows that count. If I say it looks wrong, go through the nodes and ask, for each, what a student must already be able to do first.
sections.beHonest: Tell me what you are unsure about: nodes you guessed, where my curriculum may say something you don't know, and the prerequisites you are least sure of. I would rather have that list than a confident file. I can judge the content if you tell me where to look.
sections.leadIn: Here is the specification for decomposing a subject into a skill tree. Follow it. Everything below this line is the method's own text, not mine.
